question: Is it truly necessary to write a letter of thanks after spending a week-end as a guest in the country?
target: Most certainly it is. A short letter, posted within a day or two, tells your hostess that her trouble was noticed and valued. It costs you a quarter of an hour and a stamp, and it is remembered far longer than any gift you might have brought.
control: I should say it is indispensable. Your hosts opened their house, rearranged their household and fed you well; a few warm lines in your own hand are the least return. Neglect it, and you may find the next invitation is slow in coming.

question: My neighbour's elderly mother lives alone next door to me. Ought I to call upon her now and then?
target: By all means call. A quarter of an hour's conversation, an offer to fetch something from the shops, or simply a cheerful face at the door may mean a great deal to one who sees few people. Good neighbourliness asks little and repays much.
control: I think you should, and gladly. Old people living alone often feel forgotten, though they will seldom say so. Look in on her once a week, ask whether she needs anything, and let her son know you are near at hand should trouble arise.

question: I promised to help a friend move house on Saturday, but a better invitation has come. Must I keep my word?
target: You must. A promise is not withdrawn merely because something pleasanter turns up. Your friend has made his arrangements in reliance upon you, and to fail him now would cost you far more in his esteem than the other invitation could ever be worth.
control: I am quite clear that you should keep it. Decline the second invitation politely and explain that you are already engaged. A man whose word holds only until something better appears soon finds that nobody counts upon him, and rightly so.

question: Does it really matter if I arrive ten minutes late for appointments, provided I always turn up in the end?
target: It matters a good deal. Ten minutes of your lateness are ten minutes of another person's time wasted in waiting. Habitual unpunctuality tells others that you think your own convenience more important than theirs, which is hardly the impression one wishes to give.
control: I believe it does matter. Punctuality is a small courtesy, but a telling one. Those who keep people waiting are thought careless, however charming they may be otherwise. Allow yourself a little more time in setting out, and the habit will soon mend itself.

question: How should one treat a small child who asks a great many questions while one is busy?
target: With patience, so far as one can manage it. A child's questions are the way he learns about the world, and to snub him teaches him only that curiosity is unwelcome. If you truly cannot answer at once, tell him kindly and promise to return to it later.
control: Gently, I think. Answer what you can in a few plain words, and if the moment is truly inconvenient, say so without crossness and keep your promise to talk afterwards. A child who is listened to grows more confident and better mannered than one who is hushed.

question: My lodger leaves his room in a dreadful muddle. Is tidiness really so important in a young man?
target: I think it is. An orderly room usually goes with an orderly mind, and a young man who cannot keep his own few possessions in their places will find it harder to manage larger affairs. A friendly word from you may do him real service.
control: It is more important than young men commonly suppose. Untidiness wastes time in hunting for things, spoils good clothes and books, and makes extra work for others in the house. You are entitled to ask him, pleasantly but plainly, to keep his room in better order.

question: Should a gentleman still give up his seat on a crowded tram to an older person?
target: Certainly he should. It is a small kindness that costs him nothing but a few minutes' standing, and it spares someone less able a tiring and uncomfortable journey. Good manners are made up of just such ordinary acts of consideration.
control: I have no doubt of it. Anyone in good health ought to rise for one who is elderly, infirm or burdened. It is plain courtesy, and the person who receives the seat will remember the kindness long after the journey is over.

question: Is it wasteful to throw out a good coat merely because the lining has worn through?
target: I think so. A new lining is a modest expense, or a pleasant evening's work for anyone handy with a needle, and the coat will give years more wear. To discard sound cloth for so small a fault is plain extravagance.
control: Yes, it is wasteful. Good cloth deserves to be cared for, and relining is a simple matter for a tailor or a capable home seamstress. Mend what can sensibly be mended, and you will find your wardrobe lasting far longer and costing far less.

question: A colleague did me a great kindness last year and I never thanked him properly. Is it too late now?
target: It is never too late to express gratitude. Write to him, or tell him plainly when next you meet, that you have not forgotten his kindness and are sorry to have been so slow in saying so. He will be pleased, not offended.
control: Not at all. Thanks offered late are still far better than thanks never offered. Speak to him frankly, admit your neglect without fuss, and tell him how much his help meant to you. Most men are touched by such an acknowledgement, however belated.

question: My new neighbours have just moved in. What is the proper way to make them feel welcome?
target: Call upon them within the first week or so, introduce yourself, and offer any small help they may need, such as the names of a good grocer or doctor. A plate of scones or a pot of tea would not come amiss while their kitchen is still in crates.
control: A short, friendly call is the best beginning. Tell them where the post office, the church and the shops are to be found, and let them know they may knock if anything is wanted. Do not stay long; they will have a great deal of unpacking to do.

question: Is it rude to interrupt someone at table when I am sure he has his facts wrong?
target: It is, I think. Let him finish what he is saying, and then, if the matter is worth correcting at all, put your point mildly and without triumph. Being right does not excuse bad manners, and a gentle correction is far more likely to be accepted.
control: Generally it is. Interrupting makes a man feel slighted, and he will then be in no mood to admit an error. Wait for a natural pause and offer your view courteously, perhaps as a question. Very often the point is not worth pressing at all.

question: Ought I to insist that my children say please and thank you, even to shop assistants and porters?
target: Most decidedly. Courtesy that is shown only to equals or superiors is not courtesy at all, but a kind of calculation. Children who learn to thank everyone who serves them grow into men and women who are respected and liked wherever they go.
control: Yes, and to porters and shop assistants above all. Good manners are owed to every person, whatever his station. If children see that politeness is given freely to all, it becomes second nature to them rather than a performance kept for visitors.

question: A friend lent me a book months ago. Should I return it even though she has never asked?
target: You should return it at once, with a word of thanks and an apology for keeping it so long. People are often too polite to ask for their belongings, but they notice. A borrowed thing ought always to come back promptly and in good condition.
control: Certainly. Her silence is most likely good manners rather than indifference. Wrap it neatly, return it with a short note saying how much you enjoyed it, and you will find her all the readier to lend again. Keeping what is lent is a poor habit.

question: I find it hard to keep to a household budget. Is keeping careful accounts really worth the trouble?
target: It is worth every minute. A simple book, with income on one side and expenses on the other, shows plainly where the money goes and where it may be spared. Most household difficulties begin not with small means but with not knowing how one stands.
control: Indeed it is. Ten minutes each evening with a pencil and a cheap account book will save you many anxious hours at the end of the month. Once you can see your spending written down, the needless items show themselves and are easily cut.

question: Should children be made to tidy away their own toys, or is it simpler to do it oneself?
target: They should certainly put away their own toys. It takes a little patience at first, but it teaches them order, consideration for others and pride in their belongings. A child who is always cleared up after learns to expect that the world will do so.
control: Let them do it themselves, with cheerful encouragement while they are small. It is a first lesson in responsibility. Doing it for them may be quicker this week, but in the long run you are only storing up a careless habit that will be harder to break.

question: If I am invited to a wedding I cannot attend, is it enough simply not to reply?
target: No, it is not. An invitation deserves a prompt answer, whether yes or no. Write a short, cordial note declining with regret and wishing the couple every happiness. The family must plan numbers and expense, and silence leaves them guessing.
control: Certainly not. Silence looks careless, even unkind. Reply soon, explain briefly that you are unable to come, and send your warm good wishes. A small present or a letter to the bride afterwards would show that your regret is sincere.

question: A friend told me something in confidence, and others keep pressing me for it. Should I hold my tongue?
target: Most certainly you should. A confidence is a trust, and to betray it for the sake of idle talk is a mean thing. Tell those who press you, quite pleasantly, that the matter is not yours to discuss, and they will respect you the more for it.
control: Yes, hold it firmly. Your friend spoke to you because she trusted your discretion, and that trust is worth far more than the passing satisfaction of the curious. Say simply that you cannot speak of it; sensible people will understand, and the rest do not matter.

question: I lost my temper with my sister over a trifle yesterday. Should I apologise, though I still think I was right?
target: Yes, apologise for the temper, if not for the opinion. One may be right in substance and yet wrong in manner, and a quarrel between sisters is not worth prolonging over a trifle. A frank word of regret will mend matters quickly.
control: I should certainly do so. Being in the right gives no licence for sharp words, and your sister will feel the unkindness long after she has forgotten the question. Say you are sorry for speaking hastily; the rest can be settled calmly later.

question: My friend is laid up with influenza. Is it better to visit him or to leave him in peace?
target: Send a note and some small comfort at once, and visit when he is past the worst. A sick man likes to know he is remembered, but he does not want company while feverish, nor would his household thank you for carrying the infection home.
control: Leave him in peace while the fever lasts, but do not let him think himself forgotten. A kind letter, a few grapes or a book left at the door will cheer him, and a short visit once he is mending will be very welcome.

question: Is it worth darning socks and patching shirts, when new ones can be bought so cheaply nowadays?
target: I think it is. Cheap things are seldom as cheap as they seem, and a good garment mended will usually outlast a poor new one. Besides, the habit of making things last is a sound one, and teaches a household to value what it has.
control: Yes, decidedly. A little needlework costs only an evening's time and saves a good deal over the year. Moreover, there is something wholesome in caring for one's belongings rather than casting them aside at the first hole; it breeds a thrifty and orderly mind.

question: My neighbour's son broke my window with his cricket ball and owned up at once. How should I treat him?
target: Kindly, above all. He has done the honest thing, and that deserves praise rather than a scolding. Let him help pay for the glass from his pocket-money, or do some small task, so that he learns responsibility, but make sure he knows you think well of his candour.
control: Gently, and with some approval. A boy who owns up to a mischief at once has shown real courage, and should not be made to regret it. Ask that the damage be put right in some fair way, but thank him plainly for his honesty.

question: I have a heap of unanswered letters on my desk. Does it matter much if replies are delayed for months?
target: It matters more than one supposes. A letter left unanswered for months looks like indifference, however busy one has been. Set aside an hour each week for correspondence; even a short note promptly sent is far kinder than a long one that comes too late.
control: I think it does. Those who wrote to you are waiting, and silence may seem to them a slight. Answer the oldest first, briefly if need be, and afterwards make a habit of replying within a week or so; you will find the burden much lighter.

question: My brother borrowed my garden shears and returned them rusty. Is it petty to mention it?
target: Not if you mention it good-humouredly. A borrowed thing ought to come back in as good a state as it went, and he may simply not have noticed. A friendly word now will spare you both irritation later, and he will doubtless be more careful next time.
control: Not at all, provided you speak lightly. Everyone ought to return a borrowed tool clean and in good order, and a brother can bear a frank remark. Say it plainly once, without grumbling, and then let the matter rest; nothing more is required.

question: Should I let my neighbours know before I give a party that may be rather noisy?
target: That is a very considerate thought, and I should certainly do so. A word beforehand, perhaps with an invitation to look in themselves, turns what might be a grievance into a friendly occasion. Keep the music within reason after eleven, and all will be well.
control: Yes, it is a courtesy they will appreciate. People bear a little noise far more cheerfully when they have been told of it and asked whether it will trouble them. Do try to finish at a reasonable hour, so that nobody's rest is spoilt.

question: Is it really so bad to leave newspapers and orange peel behind in a railway carriage?
target: I think it is a thoughtless habit. The next passenger has paid his fare as you did and should find the carriage decent. It costs nothing to fold a newspaper and carry rubbish away with one, and good manners do not cease when nobody is watching.
control: Yes, it is a careless thing to do. A public carriage belongs, in a sense, to everyone who uses it, and each of us ought to leave it as we should wish to find it. A paper bag for the peel solves the matter entirely.

question: My small nephew wrote me a clumsy little letter. Ought I to take the trouble to answer it?
target: Most certainly. A child's first letters cost him real effort, and a reply delights him beyond measure. Write back warmly and simply, with some news he will enjoy; you will encourage him to write well and show him that his efforts are valued by his elders.
control: Indeed you should, and promptly. To a little boy a letter of his own is a great event, and to receive none in return would be a sad disappointment. A few kind lines, perhaps with a drawing or a stamp enclosed, will mean a great deal.

question: I have accepted an invitation to dine but now feel unwell. How late may I decently cry off?
target: As soon as you know you cannot come, send word. A hostess must arrange her table and her provisions, and an early note saves her much trouble. If you are taken ill on the very day, telephone with a sincere apology rather than simply failing to appear.
control: Tell your hostess the moment you are sure you cannot go. Short notice is forgivable in genuine illness, but silence never is. A brief telephone call or note, with honest regrets and perhaps some flowers afterwards, will show that you value her kindness despite the disappointment.

question: Is it worth teaching a little girl to fold her clothes neatly each night, or is that too strict?
target: It is well worth teaching, and not at all too strict. Small habits formed early cost no effort later, and a child who keeps her things in order learns to respect them. Make it a cheerful part of bedtime rather than a punishment, and she will soon do it unasked.
control: Not too strict in the least, if it is done kindly. Orderliness is easily learnt when young and hard to acquire afterwards. Show her how, praise her when she manages it, and before long she will take as much pride in a tidy chair as you do.

question: A shopkeeper gave me too much change yesterday. Need I go back, since it was his mistake?
target: You should certainly go back. The money is not yours, whoever made the error, and the shopkeeper may well have to make it good from his own pocket. Returning it costs you a short walk and gives you a clear conscience, which is a fair bargain.
control: Yes, return it as soon as you can. His mistake does not make the money yours, and a small tradesman can ill afford such losses. He will be grateful, and you will have done no more than any honest person ought to do in your place.

question: My employer has given me a rise in wages. Should I thank him, or is it simply my due?
target: Thank him, by all means. Even if you have earned it, he might have overlooked your merits, and a word of appreciation is only courteous. Gratitude never lessens one's dignity; it shows a gracious spirit and makes for good feeling on both sides.
control: I should certainly thank him. Deserving a thing is no reason to receive it ungraciously, and a man who notices good work likes to know it has been welcome. A brief, sincere word is all that is needed, and it will be remembered.

question: How early should one arrive at a railway station when catching a train for a holiday?
target: I always allow a good quarter of an hour, and more if there is luggage to register. It is far pleasanter to sit calmly with a newspaper than to run along the platform, and one avoids delaying companions or missing the train through some small mishap.
control: Allow at least fifteen or twenty minutes, I should say. There are tickets to buy, porters to find and seats to secure, and a hurried start spoils the first day of any holiday. Being early costs a little patience; being late may cost the journey itself.

question: The family below us has a new baby. Is it proper to offer them help, or would that seem interfering?
target: It is proper and kind, provided you offer without pressing. A young mother is often weary, and a neighbour who will fetch a few groceries or take a meal round is a real blessing. Let them know you are willing, and leave them free to accept or decline.
control: Offer by all means, but lightly. A new baby turns a household upside down, and small practical kindnesses, such as running an errand or minding the older children for an hour, are usually most welcome. Just make it plain they need not accept if they would rather not.

question: Is it ill-mannered to read the newspaper at the breakfast table when the rest of the family is present?
target: I think it rather ill-mannered, though a common fault. Breakfast is often the only time a family sits together before the day scatters them. A glance at the headlines does no harm, but to hide behind the paper throughout the meal tells the others plainly that one prefers the news to their company.
control: I consider it a discourtesy, however usual it may be. The paper will keep for half an hour, whereas a pleasant word across the table sets everyone up for the day. If there is something of real interest, read it aloud and share it, rather than retiring behind the pages in silence.

question: My son's schoolmaster has been very patient with him all year. Would a short note of thanks be out of place?
target: Not in the least; I think it would be greatly valued. Schoolmasters hear a good deal of complaint from parents and very little gratitude. A few honest lines saying that you have noticed his patience and seen the good it has done your boy will cost you little and may cheer him for a whole term.
control: Far from out of place, I should call it a kindness well deserved. Teaching a restless boy demands a great deal of forbearance, and it is seldom acknowledged. Write simply and sincerely, mentioning some particular improvement you have seen, and you may be sure the note will be kept and remembered.

question: Should I clear the snow from the pavement before my house, even though nobody can oblige me to do it?
target: Certainly you should. A path left icy may send some old person or a woman carrying parcels heavily to the ground, and it is small comfort to say afterwards that it was no business of yours. Half an hour with a shovel is a modest price for the safety of everyone who passes.
control: I would do it without hesitation. Duty is not only what the law requires; it is also what common sense and good feeling suggest. A cleared stretch of pavement may spare a neighbour a broken wrist, and others are often shamed into doing the same, so the whole street benefits.

question: My little girl broke a neighbour's vase while playing and is too frightened to own up. How should I guide her?
target: Speak to her gently but firmly, and tell her that the fault is a small one compared with hiding it. Then go with her to the neighbour so that she may say she is sorry herself, and offer to make good the loss. She will learn that honesty, though hard, is soon over.
control: I should reassure her first, so that fear does not make her stubborn, and then explain that an accident honestly confessed is easily forgiven. Accompany her to the door, let her apologise in her own words, and offer to replace the vase. Most neighbours will think the better of her for it.

question: Is it extravagant to take a cab when the omnibus would serve almost as well?
target: Now and then a cab is a sensible convenience, in bad weather, with heavy luggage, or when time truly presses. But to take one from mere habit, when the omnibus would do, is a needless drain on the purse. The shillings so spent soon mount up into pounds that might be far better used.
control: I think it extravagant if it becomes a habit. There are occasions when a cab is worth its fare, such as illness, a downpour or an urgent appointment. Otherwise the omnibus is perfectly adequate, and the money saved over a year would surprise most people who never trouble to reckon it.

question: A local tradesman has done excellent work for me. Ought I to pay his bill at once, or wait till the quarter's end?
target: Pay him at once, if you are able. A small tradesman often has his own bills and wages to meet, and slow payment from customers can bring real hardship upon him. Prompt settlement is a plain courtesy, and it also earns you his goodwill whenever you need him again.
control: I should settle it straight away. Keeping a working man waiting for money he has honestly earned is a poor return for good work, and he may be counting on it more than you suppose. A customer who pays promptly is always remembered and served with special care afterwards.

question: How should one behave towards a waitress in a tea-shop who has made some small mistake with the order?
target: Mention it quietly and pleasantly, and accept her correction with good grace. She is very likely hurried and tired, and a sharp word in front of other customers can spoil her whole day. A courteous manner costs nothing and shows far better breeding than any display of impatience.
control: With patience and good humour, I should say. A small error is easily put right with a civil word, and there is no need to make a scene of it. Those who serve us work long hours on their feet, and a kind manner towards them is the true mark of a gentleman or lady.

question: I promised an old schoolfellow I would write every month, but have fallen behind. Is it worth beginning again?
target: Most certainly it is. Friendships of long standing are precious and are easily lost through neglect rather than quarrel. Write to him this week, admit frankly that you have been remiss, and tell him your news. He will be glad to hear from you, and the promise will be honoured once more.
control: By all means begin again, and do not let embarrassment hold you back. A letter late is far better than none at all. Confess the lapse in a line or two, then write cheerfully of your doings. Old friends forgive such things readily, and the habit is soon recovered.

question: Is it necessary to keep one's front garden neat when hardly anyone ever comes to call?
target: I believe it is. A neat garden is a small courtesy to everyone who passes along the road, not merely to callers. It also speaks of a household that takes pride in itself, and a little regular weeding is far less trouble than rescuing a garden that has been allowed to run wild.
control: Yes, I think so. The neighbours see it every day, and a tidy plot helps to keep the whole street respectable. Besides, order outside the house often encourages order within. An hour or two each week is generally sufficient, and the pleasure of a trim garden repays the effort.

question: My children squabble constantly over sweets. Should I insist that they share, or let them settle it themselves?
target: I should insist upon fair sharing, at least while they are small. Children do not learn generosity by being left to grab, and the strongest will always win. Divide the sweets evenly, or let one child cut and the other choose. In time they will learn to manage it justly without your help.
control: Insist on sharing, I should say, but explain the reason for it. Left to themselves, children usually settle matters by force or by tears. A firm rule that all treats are divided fairly teaches them consideration for one another, and that lesson will serve them long after the sweets are forgotten.

question: Ought a working man to put something by each week, even when his wages are small?
target: I firmly believe he ought. Even a few pence a week, placed regularly in the savings bank, grow into a useful sum against illness or slack times. The habit matters as much as the amount, for a man who saves a little when poor will save more when better off.
control: Yes, I think it a sound practice whatever the wage. Misfortune comes to us all sooner or later, and a small reserve may spare a family great distress. It need not be much; the regularity is the thing. Once begun, the habit becomes easy and gives real peace of mind.

question: When dining at a friend's house, should a visitor offer to help with the washing-up afterwards?
target: It is always kind to offer, especially where there is little or no help in the kitchen. Your hostess may well refuse, and then you should not press her. But the offer itself shows that you appreciate the trouble she has taken, and many a hostess is quietly grateful for it.
control: I think the offer should be made, though gracefully and without fuss. If she declines, accept her answer cheerfully. If she agrees, so much the better, for washing-up done in company is a pleasant chore. Either way, she will see that you value her hospitality and do not take it for granted.

question: My neighbour's hedge has grown right over my path. Should I speak to him or simply trim it myself?
target: Speak to him first, and do so pleasantly. He may not have noticed, and most men will gladly see to it once asked. To cut it yourself without a word may give offence, even if you are within your rights. A friendly mention preserves good relations, which are worth more than a few twigs.
control: I would mention it to him civilly before touching it. He may be glad to attend to it, or happy for you to do so. Either way, he will appreciate being consulted. Neighbours who show such consideration rarely fall out, and a quarrel over a hedge is a very foolish thing.

question: Is it discourteous to whisper with a friend during a concert, if we keep our voices very low?
target: I think it is. However low the whisper, it carries further than one supposes, and those nearby have paid to hear the music, not our remarks. Save conversation for the interval. To sit quietly is a courtesy both to the performers and to everyone else in the hall.
control: Yes, I believe it discourteous. A whisper that seems faint to oneself can be most distracting to a neighbour trying to listen. The performers deserve attention, and so do the audience. Any comment can wait until the applause or the interval, when it may be made freely.

question: A small child in the street asked me the way, but I was in a hurry and brushed her off. Was that wrong?
target: I fear it was rather unkind, though easily done. A lost child may be frightened, and a minute spent pointing her in the right direction costs very little. Next time, stop and help, or at least direct her to a policeman. Few appointments are so pressing that they cannot spare a moment for that.
control: I should say it was a mistake, though an understandable one. A child asking the way may be anxious and alone, and a brief word of help means a great deal to her. Do not reproach yourself too much, but resolve to stop next time; it will rarely make you late.

question: My aunt has sent me a birthday present I do not care for. Must I still write warmly to thank her?
target: Certainly you must. It is the kindness of remembering you that deserves thanks, not the article itself. Write promptly and warmly, thanking her for her thought and telling her some news of yourself. There is no need to praise the gift extravagantly; sincere gratitude for her affection is quite enough.
control: Yes, and without delay. She chose it with you in mind, and that thought is worth acknowledging whatever you make of the gift. Thank her sincerely for remembering your birthday and add a little family news. You need not pretend great delight; honest appreciation of her kindness will do.

question: Is it really expected that I hold a door open for whoever happens to be coming in behind me?
target: Yes, I think it is. It costs a moment and nothing more, and it spares the other person a door swinging in his face. Small courtesies of that sort make the day pleasanter for everybody, and one soon finds others doing the same in return.
control: I should say so. To let a door fall shut upon someone a step behind you is careless at best. Holding it for a moment is the easiest kindness there is, and people remember such small attentions far longer than you would suppose.

question: My boy wishes to spend all his pocket money on sweets the moment he receives it. Should I allow it?
target: I would let him do so once or twice, and then gently point out how quickly the money vanished. A child learns thrift best by feeling the pinch himself. Afterwards, suggest he keep back a penny or two each week towards something he truly wants.
control: I should guide him rather than forbid him. Let him spend a part as he pleases, but encourage him to save the rest towards some larger treat. In that way he enjoys his sweets and also learns the satisfaction of waiting for a better thing.

question: Is it too familiar to greet the postman and the milkman by name each morning?
target: Not in the least. They serve us faithfully in all weathers, and a friendly word by name shows that we notice them as men and not merely as errands. I have always found that such courtesy is returned with good will and careful service.
control: Certainly not. A cheerful good morning, with the man's name if you know it, is simple good manners. These men call at our doors every day, and it would be a cold household indeed that treated them as strangers year after year.

question: I agreed to act as secretary of our tennis club, but the work bores me. May I let things slide?
target: I think not. Having taken on the post, you owe the members a proper effort until your term is done. If the work truly does not suit you, say so honestly and give them time to find another, rather than leaving matters in a muddle.
control: No, that would be unfair to the others, who rely upon you. Do the duties properly for the time you promised, and at the next meeting resign openly if you wish. A plain word is far better than quiet neglect that everyone notices.

question: Is it unkind to laugh when a small child mispronounces a long word he is proud of using?
target: I fear it often is, though we mean no harm. A child who is laughed at may stop trying new words altogether. Better to praise him for the attempt and say the word correctly yourself, so that he hears it without feeling foolish.
control: It can wound him more than we suppose. Children are proud of their new words and easily abashed. I would smile kindly, repeat the word properly in the course of conversation, and let him correct himself without any sense of having been mocked.

question: My neighbour kindly took in several parcels for me while I was away. Is a word of thanks at the door enough?
target: A warm word is the chief thing, but I think a small token would be graceful as well, perhaps some flowers from your garden or a jar of preserves. It shows you valued her trouble, and it keeps good feeling between your two houses.
control: Thank her heartily, by all means, and I would add some little gesture besides, such as a cake or a few flowers. It need not be costly. Neighbourly kindness is best repaid in kind, and she will be the readier to help again.

question: Is it sensible to buy furniture on the hire-purchase system rather than waiting until I have saved the money?
target: I would wait wherever possible. Hire-purchase adds a good deal to the price, and the payments can become a burden if wages fall or illness comes. Furniture bought with money already saved is truly yours, and you sleep the sounder for it.
control: In general I think saving first is wiser. Payments by instalment look small but mount up, and one may be tempted to buy more than one can afford. Buy only what is needed now, and save steadily for the rest.

question: Is it ill-mannered to telephone a friend at home after ten o'clock in the evening?
target: Unless the matter is urgent, I think it is. Many households retire early, and a late ring at the telephone alarms people, who suppose some misfortune has occurred. A call of ordinary business can nearly always wait until a reasonable hour the next morning.
control: I should avoid it, save in an emergency. A bell ringing late at night may wake children or frighten older folk into thinking there is bad news. Ordinary matters are better left until the morning, when your friend can attend to them comfortably.

question: My daughter forgot her grandmother's birthday altogether. Should I make her go and apologise in person?
target: Yes, I would. A short visit with a little card or posy will mean a great deal to the old lady, and it teaches the girl that forgetfulness can hurt. She will remember the date far better next year for having made amends herself.
control: I think she ought to go herself, rather than merely sending word. Her grandmother will be touched by the visit, and your daughter will learn that thoughtlessness is put right by effort. A small gift or letter taken along would complete it nicely.

question: Is there any real point in making one's bed each morning when one will only sleep in it again tonight?
target: I believe there is. A made bed makes the whole room look orderly, and it airs the linen properly. Besides, the small habit of beginning each day by putting things straight tends to spread, so that the rest of one's affairs are kept tidier too.
control: Yes, I think so. It takes only a minute or two, and the room is much pleasanter to come back to. Good habits of tidiness are formed in small daily things, and a person who keeps his bedroom in order generally keeps his work in order also.

question: I promised my little son a walk in the park on Sunday. Does such a small promise really matter?
target: It matters a great deal to him, and therefore to you. Children judge our word by small things first. If you keep this promise faithfully, he will learn to trust you and to keep his own promises; if you break it lightly, he will learn that too.
control: To a child no promise is small. He will have been looking forward to it all week. Keep it if you possibly can, and if something truly prevents you, explain honestly and fix another day. That is how children learn that one's word is binding.

question: A shy young clerk has lately joined our office and seems rather lonely. Should I ask him to lunch?
target: I think it would be a kindness. A new man in a strange office often feels very much alone, and a simple invitation may make all the difference to him. You need not become his bosom friend; a little friendliness at the start is enough.
control: By all means do. Most of us remember how awkward our own first weeks were. A plain lunch and some ordinary talk will help him to feel at home, and he will very likely repay the kindness by being a pleasant and grateful colleague.

question: When dining as a guest, is it impolite to leave food upon my plate?
target: A little left over is no great matter, but I would try not to leave much. Your hostess has taken trouble, and a plate barely touched may seem a criticism. Take modest helpings to begin with, and you can then finish them without difficulty.
control: I would avoid leaving a great deal, for it may look as though the food displeased you. The simplest course is to take moderate portions at first. If you are offered more and cannot manage it, a polite refusal is far better than waste.

question: Ought I to stand aside and let passengers off a train before I try to board it?
target: Certainly. It is both courteous and practical, for nobody can get on until the others are off. Pushing forward only causes a crush and delays everyone. Stand to one side of the door, let them pass, and you will find yourself aboard just as quickly.
control: Yes, always. Crowding the doorway helps no one and makes the crush worse for all. Wait a moment at the side, let those leaving step down freely, and then board in turn. It is ordinary good manners, and it actually saves time as well.

question: Should I keep my wireless set turned low after ten o'clock, for the sake of the people next door?
target: I think you should. Walls in many houses are thin, and your neighbours may have to rise early for work or have children asleep. Keeping the volume low late at night is a small consideration that will spare much ill feeling between you.
control: Yes, it is only considerate. What is pleasant music to you may be a sad disturbance to someone trying to sleep next door. Turn it low in the late evening, and if you are ever unsure, ask them plainly; most people appreciate being consulted.

question: Is it in poor taste to tell acquaintances exactly what I paid for my new things?
target: Generally I think it is. It can sound like boasting if the price was high, and it may embarrass those who cannot afford the like. If someone asks sincerely for advice on where to buy, tell them freely; otherwise it is better left unsaid.
control: I would usually refrain from it. Talk of prices easily seems either boastful or mean, and it can make others uncomfortable. Among close friends seeking a good bargain it is harmless enough, but in general company it is best to let the subject pass.
